title: Eight Historic Bathhouses
text: Eight historic bathhouses stand on Bathhouse Row: Superior, Hale, Maurice, Fordyce, Quapaw, Ozark, Buckstaff and Lamar, lining Central Avenue.

title: The Oldest on the Row
text: The Hale, built in 1892–93, is the oldest surviving bathhouse on the Row. The Buckstaff (1912), Fordyce (1914–15) and Lamar (1923) came later.

title: Baths Since 1912
text: The Buckstaff opened on February 1, 1912, and NPS says it has offered baths in continuous operation ever since.

title: The Priciest Bathhouse
text: The Fordyce, the most elaborate and most expensive bathhouse, cost $212,749.55 to build in 1914–15, including fixtures and furniture.

title: Under the Skylight
text: The Fordyce's massive stained-glass skylight is in the men's area, with the DeSoto Fountain centered on the floor directly below it.

title: Horseshoe and Magnesia
text: The 1922 Quapaw Bathhouse was built on the sites of two earlier bathhouses, the Horseshoe and the Magnesia.

title: Shells and Sculpin
text: Sculpin fish decorate the Quapaw's parapets, framed by scalloped shells. The fish were originally gold and are now white.

title: Two Bronze Eagles
text: Two bronze federal eagles guard Bathhouse Row's 1890s main entrance. Army engineer Lt. Robert Stevens designed the reservation's entrances.

title: A Course of 21 Baths
text: In 1920 a standard prescribed "course" at Hot Springs was 21 baths, and a course cost $9 to $15.

title: The Row Completed
text: The final change to Bathhouse Row was completed when the Lamar opened in 1923, NPS says. The Lamar closed in 1985.

title: Forty-Seven Springs
text: USGS says the park is best known for its 47 hot springs, which emerge from Hot Springs Mountain at an average temperature of 143°F.

title: Hottest East of the Rockies
text: NPS calls the Hot Springs thermal springs the hottest east of the Rocky Mountains. They average about 143°F.

title: Rain from Long Ago
text: USGS tritium and carbon-14 dating show most of the thermal water is about 4,400 years old, mixed with a very small amount under 20 years old.

title: Heated a Mile Down
text: Rainwater heats to about 160°F through the geothermal gradient, roughly a mile underground, before it rises again as spring water.

title: The Alpha and Beta Faults
text: NPS says two faults, named alpha and beta, help direct the heated water back up to the surface.

title: 700,000 Gallons a Day
text: The National Park Service says the thermal springs produce over 700,000 gallons of water a day.

title: Tufa Rock
text: Minerals dissolved in the spring water precipitate near the spring openings as white-to-tan travertine, or tufa rock.

title: The Display Spring
text: The Display Spring was covered by a grate for decades. In the 1930s it was uncovered so visitors could see thermal water in its natural state.

title: The Grand Promenade
text: The Grand Promenade, a National Recreation Trail and the entry point to the park from downtown, is about half a mile long.
source: NPS: Hot Springs & North Mountain Trails

title: A 216-Foot Tower
text: The Hot Springs Mountain Tower is 216 feet tall. The lattice steel observation tower officially opened to the public on June 3, 1983.

title: Valley Street
text: Central Avenue was originally Valley Street. By the late 1870s it was named Central Avenue to reflect its status as the commercial center.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Central Avenue Historic District

title: The Third Arlington
text: After the 1923 fire, work on the third Arlington Hotel began Oct. 25, 1923, and the new hotel was completed Nov. 28, 1924.

title: Kome To Hot Springs
text: The call letters of Hot Springs radio station KTHS stood for "Kome (Come) To Hot Springs."
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: KTHS Radio Station

title: Radio at the Arlington
text: KTHS first broadcast from the Arlington Hotel. The station was built on the new Arlington's upper floor.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: KTHS Radio Station

title: Lum and Abner
text: The radio comedy team Lum and Abner first performed on KTHS in April 1931, at a flood relief benefit that launched their careers.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: KTHS Radio Station

title: The Southern Club, 1893
text: The Southern Club on Central Avenue was built in 1893 as a private club by Charles Dugan and Dan Stuart.

title: Dark Pittsburgh Glass
text: After William Jacobs bought the Southern Club building in 1927, he encased its front in dark Pittsburgh glass, which helped hide the gambling.

title: The Ohio Club, 1905
text: The Ohio Club on Central Avenue was founded in 1905. During Prohibition it officially became the Ohio Cigar Store, a front with a fake wall.

title: The Shortest Street
text: In the 1940s, Ripley's Believe It or Not designated Hot Springs' Bridge Street "the shortest street in the world."
source: ACHP: The Hot Springs National Park Visitors Center

title: Scotch and Soda
text: Mayor Leo McLaughlin's sulky was pulled down Central Avenue by horses named Scotch and Soda. He rode daily, wearing a red carnation.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Leo P. McLaughlin

title: Spring Training, 1886
text: Hot Springs first welcomed Major League Baseball in 1886, when the Chicago White Stockings came to town for spring training.

title: Whittington Park, 1894
text: Hot Springs' Whittington Park ballfield opened in 1894. It replaced the Hot Springs Baseball Grounds.

title: Into the Alligator Farm
text: Babe Ruth's famous long home run of March 17, 1918, at Whittington Park landed in the Arkansas Alligator Farm, Wikipedia says.

title: About 573 Feet
text: A 2011 engineering measurement put Ruth's 1918 Whittington Park homer at about 573 feet. A Boston paper had thought it went more than 500.
source: KNWA/KFTA: The home run that made Babe Ruth a star

title: Ban Johnson Park
text: In 1935 Whittington Park was renamed for Hall of Fame baseball pioneer Ban Johnson, founder of the American League.

title: The First Umpire School
text: Hot Springs' George Barr school (1935–47) is recognized as the first school for umpires in baseball.

title: 1904 or 1905?
text: Sources disagree on when Oaklawn opened: Wikipedia says Feb. 24, 1904; the Encyclopedia of Arkansas says Feb. 15, 1905.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Oaklawn Park; Wikipedia: Oaklawn Racing Casino Resort

title: A City Holiday
text: Hot Springs declared a city holiday for Oaklawn's first day of racing, and more than 3,000 people attended, per Wikipedia.

title: The First Arkansas Derby
text: The first Arkansas Derby was run at Oaklawn in 1936, for a purse of $5,000.

title: The Fifth Season
text: Wikipedia says the Oaklawn race meet, held December through May, is sometimes called the "Fifth Season."

title: Carpenter Dam, 1931
text: Arkansas Power & Light developed Lake Hamilton. Its Carpenter Dam, a concrete gravity dam, was completed in 1931, and the lake was created in 1932.

title: About 7,200 Acres
text: Lake Hamilton covers about 7,200 acres. Lake Catherine, the smaller of the two lakes, is about 1,940 acres.

title: Creek to Lake
text: Hot Springs Creek flows from Whittington Avenue through the southern city and, after passing under Bathhouse Row, empties into Lake Hamilton.

title: Remmel Dam, 1924
text: Remmel Dam, built in 1924, forms Lake Catherine. Remmel and Carpenter dams were both listed on the National Register in 1992.

title: Blakely Mountain Dam
text: The Army Corps of Engineers built the 231-foot Blakely Mountain Dam from 1948 to 1953. It creates Lake Ouachita.

title: Two Hundred Islands
text: Lake Ouachita has about 200 islands, according to Wikipedia's infobox for the lake.

title: Three Sisters Springs
text: Lake Ouachita State Park, a 360-acre park that opened in 1955, preserves the historic healing springs called Three Sisters Springs.

title: Winter Eagles
text: In January and February, eagle-watch cruises at Lake Ouachita State Park look for bald eagles.
source: Arkansas Democrat-Gazette: Eagle-watching excursions take off at state parks (2019)

title: Trout Below the Dam
text: From November through April, the AGFC stocks catchable rainbow trout in the Ouachita River tailwaters below Carpenter Dam.

title: The State Mineral
text: Quartz crystal became Arkansas's state mineral in 1967, when Gov. Winthrop Rockefeller signed Act 128 on Feb. 22, 1967.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Official State Mineral

title: Visitor Center, 1989
text: The Fordyce closed on June 29, 1962. Since 1989 it has served as the visitor center of Hot Springs National Park.

title: Quapaw Baths Reopen
text: NPS restored the Quapaw Bathhouse in 2004, and Quapaw Baths & Spa opened in the building in July 2008.

title: The Ozark's New Life
text: The Ozark Bathhouse reopened in 2014 as the Hot Springs National Park Cultural Center, showing artist-in-residence work.

title: Hotel Hale
text: NPS says the Hale Bathhouse is now Hotel Hale, with nine suites whose soaking tubs get hot springs mineral water.

title: Restoring the Maurice
text: Work on the Maurice Bathhouse, about $31.6 million, broke ground Aug. 19, 2025. It is the last building on the Row to be rehabilitated.
source: NPS: Groundbreaking celebrated for Maurice Bathhouse rehabilitation

title: Running of the Tubs
text: Racers push bathtubs the length of Bathhouse Row. Visit Hot Springs billed the 2026 races as the 20th running since they began in 2006.
source: Visit Hot Springs: Running of the Tubs 2026 press release

title: 210 Acres of Garden
text: Garvan Woodland Gardens on Lake Hamilton covers 210 acres. The University of Arkansas owns the garden.

title: Anthony Chapel
text: Anthony Chapel, a wood-and-glass chapel in Garvan Woodland Gardens by Maurice Jennings and David McKee, officially opened in September 2006.
source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Garvan Woodland Gardens

title: 150,000 Tulips
text: About 150,000 tulips bloom in Garvan Woodland Gardens' Tulip Extravaganza, mid-March to mid-April in the Sensory Garden, per Visit Hot Springs.
source: Visit Hot Springs: A reason to visit every season

title: Nearly 5 Million Lights
text: Garvan Woodland Gardens' multi-week Holiday Lights display features nearly 5 million lights, Visit Hot Springs says.
source: Visit Hot Springs: A reason to visit every season
